title: An interdimensional funnel enhances topologically protected oscillations in high-dimensional stochastic systems
abstract: Biochemical systems such as protein complexes often occupy configuration spaces whose dimensionality grows with the number of molecular components. Although usually viewed as an obstacle to coherent dynamics, here we show that high dimensionality can enhance topologically protected oscillations. In the topological regime, a stochastic system with a $D$-dimensional configuration space develops a steady-state current confined to a one-dimensional edge cycle. The intervening boundary faces between the $D$-dimensional bulk and the one-dimensional cycle form an interdimensional funnel, sequentially pushing the system towards lower dimensional faces, down to the one-dimensional cycle. As a consequence, increasing $D$ enhances the funnel, leading to improved one-dimensional localization and oscillatory coherence. A quantized biorthogonal Zak phase identifies the transition to the topological regime, which additionally exhibits a highly structured non-Hermitian skin effect. In contrast with previous realizations of topological states in stochastic systems, the phenomena we uncover have no counterpart in quantum condensed matter or active matter systems.
summary: This work demonstrates that in high-dimensional stochastic systems, the geometry of the state space—specifically the 'interdimensional funnel'—can enhance topological protection. By increasing dimensionality, the system's steady-state probability becomes increasingly localized onto a coherent one-dimensional cycle, a phenomenon unique to stochastic systems and not found in standard quantum models.
main_problem: The paper investigates how high dimensionality can enhance topologically protected oscillations in stochastic systems, contrary to the expectation that high dimensions complicate dynamics.
main_result: Increasing the dimensionality ($D$) enhances an 'interdimensional funnel,' leading to improved one-dimensional localization and enhanced oscillatory coherence in the steady state.
method: The analysis uses stochastic simulation (Gillespie method) alongside rigorous spectral analysis of the transition matrix to characterize localization and coherence.
model_or_system: The system is modeled as a continuous-time Markov process on a configuration space defined by a hypercubic lattice of dimension $D$, incorporating both external and internal transitions.
key_observables: Localization measures ($	ext{Ploc}$, $	ext{floc}$), oscillation coherence (Period Precision $N$, Spectral Coherence $R$), and the steady-state probability distribution.
important_parameters: Dimensionality ($D$), the ratio of transition rates ($\gamma_{ex}/\gamma_{in}$), and the system size ($N$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes a specific structure for the stochastic dynamics (hypercubic lattice, ring-like internal states) and analyzes the system in the topological regime ($\gamma_{ex}/\gamma_{in} > 1$).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate stochastic trajectories showing the funneling effect from the bulk to a 1D cycle, and compare steady-state probabilities across varying dimensions ($D$).
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the physical model and the counter-intuitive result (high D enhances coherence) to detailed mathematical analysis using spectral theory to prove the isolation of the steady-state band and characterize the mode structure.
why_interesting: The findings provide a novel mechanism where high dimensionality, instead of causing decoherence, structures the dynamics into highly coherent, low-dimensional topological cycles, which has implications for understanding complex biological or active matter systems.
